utterances.text: Will you agree with me, since you are an experienced policeman, that there was reason to believe that you were linked to the armed formations, that you were armed, that you had hand grenades, that there was reason to suspect that you had shot at the barracks in Djakovo and that you were a member of the armed formations of the SDA and HDZ? Do you agree with this statement of mine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of the armed forces of Muslims and Croats. I was a reserve policeman of the Bosanski Samac police station, which represented legal authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge and experience in the capacity of professional policeman, I'm asking you whether, based on everything that I just described to you, all the reasons to suspect you and all the circumstances, do you believe that there was reason to arrest you and to bring you in for interrogation? We have somebody who possesses hand grenades, who has an automatic weapon, perhaps has been in contact with enemy forces. Is that a reasonable grounds for arresting somebody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I object. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Wait. Wait before you answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Pantelic is trying to establish is whether or not Stiv Todorovic had reasonable cause to arrest this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If he wants to go down that road, let him. I have no problem with that. But the last part of the question is that automatic weapons, contact with enemy forces, and so on, and the witness hasn't said anything. He says that Todorovic -- any of that. Todorovic merely said, according to him -- accused him, that the witness is shooting at barracks, where there was fighting in Djakovo. Now, that's the -- yes, that's -- Ms. Reidy points out in another country. So that's the -- that's all that the witness said, and it's -- if Mr. Pantelic wants to explore whether or not shooting at barracks in Djakovo is reasonable cause for Stevan Todorovic to arrest him, well, perhaps that might in some vague, indistinct way be relevant. I don't know. But there's nothing that the witness said in his statement about automatic weapons, grenades, or anything like that. It's a complicated issue and I really don't know why the witness is being called upon to comment on Stiv Todorovic's mind or what Stiv Todorovic thought was reasonable or not. It's very difficult to know. So -- but to be fair to the witness, all he said is Todorovic accused him of shooting at barracks. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. You understand the objection of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand, but I disagree with this approach, and I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps you can rephrase your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I think I was quite clear, because I tried to establish the previous experience of this person, of Witness A, being professional policeman, and then with several details. I'm not entering into the discussion whether the certain allegations were truthful or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm not challenging that. I'm just asking from the point of view -- can I finish, please? I'm just asking from the point of view of one person who is a professional policeman whether, according to his experience and knowledge, certain details, not to enter into the validity of these events, will be sufficient for the police force to, let's say, arrest someone or to conduct investigation, et cetera, et cetera. Very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very innocent, Your Honour. I'm not telling -- I'm not putting to this witness that he's shooting on the barracks. I'm not putting to this witness -- well, he confirmed that -- he confessed that he got two grenades, one Kalashnikov, a pistol. Well, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it's a general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a general question from his point of view, of his experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: His experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Whether if someone is working on the street, you know, especially in the wartime, or whether the police officer, knowing that someone is in possession of the weapons or have some other -- I don't know which kind of information of the organisation or stuff like that. And then is that a sufficient ground to call someone -- prima facie case to call someone to discuss that. Nothing more. Simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand all of that and I've got no quarrel with it. So why can't the question simply be dealt with quickly, perhaps putting it along these lines: Did Stevan Todorovic, in your opinion, have reasonable grounds for arresting you on the basis of an allegation that you were shooting at barracks in Djakovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I just said, Your Honour, in my question. It was in my question in the transcript. I phrased the question on the same way and same standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You can check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's stop this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let's go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you ask the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you rephrase it? Ask the question again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, so we are not here trying to establish whether it is true whether you indeed did shoot and so on. We're not interested in that at all. All I'm asking you is whether you, as an experienced policeman, believe that if there are reasons to believe that somebody has illegal weapons or has joined an illegal armed organisation or has committed a crime, is that sufficient to bring in somebody for an interrogation and to initiate certain investigative procedures? I'm repeating, sir, that I fully understand that everything that happened to you from that point on was beyond belief and beyond reason, but we're not interested in that. All we're interested in is whether, in accordance with the police standards, in accordance with your police experience, it is acceptable to bring in somebody for interrogation if there are all of these reasons to suspect that there was some wrongdoing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a yes or no reply to this question. Let me tell you this: At that time the weapons that I had at the time were legally registered with MUP. I possessed legal weapons. I had a permit. I was a member of police force. And Stevan Todorovic arrested us illegally. So he was not authorised to bring me in for questioning. I will simply not accept this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you just one more question and then we will be finished shortly thereafter. Please turn to page 10 of your 1994 statement. In last paragraph, which will be paragraph 4 of that statement, you mentioned certain inmates, such as Luka Gregurevic, Ivica Evic, Mato Senic, Cutura?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Kemal Atic, Barukcic, and so on. Let me ask you this: Was Luka Gregurevic, who is a policeman, in prison together with you? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was on duty that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Is Mato Senic a policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, in accordance with the duty roster, Mato was securing --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that. Was he a member of police force or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you go through that statement and tell me if any of these other persons you mentioned were policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Salko Hurtic, Cosic, Barukcic, Kemal Atic, Ibrahim Salkic, Ilija Matic, Anto Orsolic were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So let's just clarify this for the sake of the transcript. Policemen who were arrested and imprisoned were Luka Gregurevic? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not arrested. I just want to clarify this for the Trial Chamber. Luka Gregurevic was on duty that night, starting at 2200 hours until 6.00 a.m. He was securing -- or rather, securing the police station from the outside, where the reserve policemen Seric, called Cutura, from Zasavica, and Salko Hurtic from Samac. And when the paramilitaries attacked Samac, they arrested them the first, on their police duty posts. And the other individuals, the civilians, which are Kemal Atic, Esad Cosic, Franjo Barukcic, Ibrahim Salkic, Dzevad Jusufovic, Anto Orsolic, and Ilija Matic, were arrested as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now please turn to page 12 of your 1994 statement, paragraph 3 counting from above, in which you mention Dikan Brandic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a tragic event and we don't need to go into details. It's been covered sufficiently here, but I found something quite interesting, something that you stated in 1994 to the Prosecution. Namely, you said that Dikan was not physically strong, but he was insolent a bit, and he would retort. So you go on to say, in the beginning of your paragraph, that the only prisoner who talked back to them was Dikan Brandic, who was later killed. What I'm interested in is this, and please correct me if I'm wrong: The late Dikan, was he brave and provocative and did he offer resistance to the paramilitaries in the TO building? Did he talk back to them? Did he act in a different manner from the rest of you? Did I understand the description of this person well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That question -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you then agree with me, based on your personal knowledge, that this behaviour of his in fact provoked the paramilitaries, or rather, Lugar and the others, into beating and killing him in the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... won't be allowed. This witness can't answer that, and it's of no consequence whether he provoked anybody, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I've almost finished with the questioning. Just a couple of questions of the personal profile and credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness A, you stated that you were an agent of Croatia, insurance agency in Samac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Before April 17th, 1992, in view of the fact that your company had a good business, as did the insurance agency, you had quite a lot of money on your company's account, because the business was good?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was money on the account, but it disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Based on the business policy of your company, you gave loans, short-term loans, to various companies and individuals, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in business policy of Croatia insurance agency. I was simply their representative selling insurance policies, and I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And what's the relevance of this, Mr. Pantelic? I think you are finished with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness A, did you, through your agency in Bosanski Samac, give short-term loans to individuals and companies? Please reply briefly, with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as an insurance salesman, somebody who insured vehicles, property, and so on, was in charge of selling insurance policies, collecting money for that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Let me rephrase the question. Did your head office perhaps issue loans, short-term loans, to companies and individuals in Samac before 1992? It's a simple question. Please give me a straight answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That was the last question, Mr. Pantelic. That was the last question. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now it's last, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a very important question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Related to the credibility of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Sit down, Mr. Pantelic. You've been given enough time. Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let's clear up this Namik Suljic business.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Have you still got the 1994 statement there, Witness? You have your 1994 statement? Do you still have it before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go back to the portion of the statement that Mr. Pantelic took you to, where you were discussing the second interrogation that you had with Milos Savic. I'll read out to you the portion of the statement to you, and I'll read it out slowly, and listen to me carefully, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me the number of the page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't, but I have your English statement, which is your signed statement, the statement that you gave. That is only a translation. So please listen to what I've got to say. Listen through the earphones and you'll be able to hear -- you may find it around page 13, but in any event --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can I help the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because I have copy of B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking anything, Your Honours; just to help. [Interpretation] Page 13, end of paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Somewhere in that paragraph, no doubt, your statement commences in this fashion, and I'll quote it to you: "The first time he was questioning me and taking notes, the second time his objective was to take a full statement from me. I was also asked to talk about anything I may have remembered in the meantime. He asked whether I had any insurance money for the kiosk that was demolished in the bombing. I told him I did not, that I did not apply for money. Since he insisted on a list of names of people in Slatina who possessed guns, I gave him a list of names of people who I was certain were not there. I put my brother Pero's name on the list because I knew he was not there, and I thought it would be proof to him that I was on the level and was telling the truth. I memorised the list of names and gave the same list again at Batajnica. Then he wanted to know what I knew about Muslims trafficking weapons across the Sava River. I asked what he wanted from me, why couldn't he see that I had been beaten and didn't know anything. He went to consult with Simo Zaric and returned with a piece of paper with questions he was supposed to ask me. He asked who was importing the guns from Croatia for Bosnian Muslims. I said all this was organised by Namik Suljic and Ragib Hodzic, a police detective from Sarajevo. I mentioned their names because I knew they could never reach them. I knew a lot about what the people in power in the SDA and HDZ were doing, but I never said anything about it." Now, is that what you said in your statement of 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you there providing and feeding information to Savic in order to placate him, to keep him happy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Does that apply to the names Namik Suljic and Ragib Hodzic that you gave to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked questions this afternoon by Mr. Pantelic regarding a portion of your statement from 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry. Will Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And Mr. Pantelic directed you to a portion of the statement in which you mention that Alija Fitozovic was dedicated to -- delegated to his position in the TO by the SDA, and Bozanovic by the HDZ. He did not read the next sentence to you, which I now do: "The Serbs did not want to delegate their own member of the Territorial Defence leadership." Is that in fact the position, that the Serbs did not want to delegate their own member to the TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked questions by another Defence counsel, Mr. Lukic, regarding mention of Franjo Barukcic in your various statements, and he directed your attention to your statement in 1994, and I think you recall that I conceded that, on your behalf, that the arrest by Mr. Tadic of Barukcic was not mentioned in that statement. And he also asked you questions on that topic and whether you mentioned Franjo Barukcic's arrest by Tadic last year, when Prosecutors came down to Odzak and asked you questions. Do you recall that portion of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he told me that he had been arrested by Miro Brko. Now, whether I stated this in my last year's statement, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine. Okay. All I want to know is this: In the statement that you gave in 1994 to investigators, and last year, when you were spoken to by the Prosecutors in Odzak, did you decide what topics you would speak about or were you directed by investigators or Prosecutors to topics that they were interested in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some corrections and the translation wasn't that good. Remember that example with Bosanski Brod and also in another place it said that I was employed as a soccer referee and so on. So there were some clarifications given, and I don't remember whether they asked me, and if they did, whether I replied, but I know for a fact that Mr. Barukcic told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just an intervention to the transcript. The witness just said, in page 57, line 4, clarification given by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm grateful to my learned friend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And in May of this year, did my colleague Ms. Reidy, who is sitting next to me, come and speak to you in Bosnia and take a further statement from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And again on that occasion did she direct your attention to areas that she was interested in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she had the statement before her, and some things weren't clear to her had, and then she asked. Some parts of the translation were not very good, but she avoided bringing me back to the things that I had been through. Again they asked me to talk about the things that I saw and the things that I heard, and the things that I didn't see myself were deleted. I see here in some translations Barukcic is mentioned as being 65, and on another occasion he is mentioned as being 85. There was a young lad doing it. He may be not so good. But I have to note that she never once asked me to say things that were not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Glad to hear that. But my question is really very simple: When she came down and saw you in May, did she direct your attention to matters that she was interested in and she was seeking clarification of? That's all. That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some things were not in good order, chronological order, and then we agreed about that and about who was with me and so on. But this was not in the way in which I gave the statement in 1994. That was more like a conversation. I was just saying things. But the things that I said to Ms. Aisling Reidy, I said it in my own words, without any premeditation, any pressure. She just asked me: Tell us the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness A. We have completed your evidence and you are free to leave. Can the witness be led out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, may I ask the witness to remain in the precincts of the Court? I want to discuss something with him following -- and I'm concerned that he'll be taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps you may -- the usher, when he escorts him out, yes, he can make sure that he waits for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Because I understand that Defence counsel want to briefly raise something now, so I won't be able to immediately exit the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. We are in open session, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to be brief, but we sit until 1900 hours, in light of our today's schedule. I think I will need ten minutes. I have two things, two motions that I would like to address to this Trial Chamber. One I will discuss at length and the other one I will just touch upon briefly. So I just want to clarify whether there will be a break or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's not possible to have a break and then come back before 1900 hours. In any case, we've been going on -- we're supposed to break off at 1840, because that would have been one and a half hours, because the interpreters will be overworked. But you can go ahead and see how far we shall go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm addressing you on behalf of the three Defence counsel. As regards the first motion and the second motion, I'm addressing you only on behalf of the Tadic and Zaric Defence, because this concerns the issue of reciprocal disclosure. In light of the testimony by witness Hasan Subasic and the allegations he made on the 17th of July, that is yesterday, 17th of July, 2002, about the fact that he watched this trial over the Internet, in response to questions asked by attorney Lazarevic and the previous day to questions asked by attorney Pantelic, the Defence asked that his testimony be stricken off the record for the following reasons: The principle of fair trial is one of the basic norms stemming from Article 21(2) of the Statute. We heard from this witness, on page 94/14 of the draft transcript, that he didn't follow all the trials but that he did follow quite a few of them. And when prompted by my colleague Mr. Lazarevic whether by that he meant the Samac case, he confirmed it. Then he explained that he followed the trial with a 30-minute delay, which means that by watching the image broadcast live from this courtroom, he was able to follow the course of the proceedings before he testified. He also confirmed that, among other things, he watched the testimony of witness Dragan Delic, Nusret Hadzijusufovic, Safet Dagovic. So he watched the testimony of witnesses that he was asked questions about in the course of the examination-in-chief, his examination-in-chief. Your Honours, the provision contained in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which is in force in all the legal systems throughout the world, that the witness must not communicate with other witnesses before his testimony, with other witnesses who had already testified, and in particular, that the witness, such a witness, is not allowed to follow the trial, is there to ensure a fair trial. It is quite clear that everybody can watch the course of the trial when it is conducted in open session over the Internet. We have an absolutely -- it's the same situation as if we had that person sitting here in the public gallery. I believe that if you watch it over the Internet, it's even better, because you get a much better picture with all the camera angles than if you were sitting in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow this, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Trial Chamber is of the view that this is an important motion. Can the parties make it in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honours. If you can set a deadline for us now, we will be submitting this motion in writing. We are quite prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps by 4.00 p.m. Wednesday next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sufficient time to putting in writing. And then the Prosecution would be required to respond, perhaps by Friday. If you receive it on Wednesday afternoon next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we receive -- if it's filed by 4.00 on Wednesday, we normally get it sometime on Thursday. I think the Rules do allow us seven days, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but we are looking at how much time we have, and since you --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Effectively be 24 hours and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Since you've heard part of it so you know where it is going.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Monday?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Monday or -- I don't know if Defence already know what they have to say. Perhaps they could file it by close of Tuesday and then we could try to file it by close of Friday. If you prefer to have it filed by the time the Court goes into recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we go back a day. By Tuesday 4.00 p.m.? Okay. We'll leave it on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can make a commitment, since we already have some written notes, I believe that we will be able to comply with the Tuesday evening deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. In which case the Prosecution will have it by Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then you would be able to file by 4.00 p.m. Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. The other point, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second motion is much shorter, but I think that I really have to speak about it at length. Perhaps it would be better to do so on Tuesday morning. It's about our motion for the Prosecution to disclose to us the documents that Ewa Tabeau used during her cross-examination pertaining to the documents that their statistics service has. It is obvious that these are very important documents, containing important statistical data that she used when making her report. These are documents that, pursuant to Rule 66, are subject to reciprocal disclosure because they're important for the Defence. I did not address this motion directly to the Prosecution. Perhaps I may approach the Prosecution directly with this motion. But I believe that it is important for the Trial Chamber to be seized of this, because our statistics expert does not have the documents at our disposal and the Prosecution is under the obligation to provide us with the documents which would enable us to check all the facts and all the data contained therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sure that can be arranged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the parties can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I think Ms. Tabeau is in fact interested in the topic herself as well, so she can easily get together the stuff that she relied on in producing her report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Her report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So let me suggest that we deal with this privately, and if we can't sort it out amongst ourselves, then we'll come back to the Chamber, but I'm sure we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'll leave it to the parties to sort out this, and then if there is any problem, the matter can always be raised with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall adjourn. Next week we are sitting in the morning, from 0900 hours. And on the 22nd it's the case of Mr. Milan Simic. We don't know how long it will take, but probably the other parties in this case will be notified as soon as possible when it will be possible to resume this particular case. The Court will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of July 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.44 p.m.,
